title: Build a safe custom-channel capacity runner
value: Let students and researchers supply a channel matrix and receive a reproducible capacity report instead of editing experiment source. This creates a useful foundation for a future visual Channel Lab while keeping the first change small.
why_now: The current README explicitly says the solvers assume valid inputs, and inspection of both solver functions confirms they immediately unpack the matrix shape and calculate probabilities without explicit validation. A small validated command-line wrapper has a concrete user benefit and can be checked against the existing analytic examples. It is a better first step than a larger visual interface or an Android feature requiring device verification. This is a proposal based on source review; no solver tests or implementation changes were performed during this planning review.
effort: About 2-4 hours, depending on the existing test setup
steps: Add a small wrapper that accepts a JSON matrix and validates nonempty two-dimensional shape, finite nonnegative entries, and row sums close to one. Reject invalid matrices with clear messages instead of silently normalizing them.
Expose standard and relaxed solver modes through one command, with explicit tolerance and iteration limits. Label tolerance and gap in nats and capacity in bits per channel use.

Write a machine-readable result containing the selected method, capacity, final gap, iterations, and a convergence flag based on the requested tolerance. Do not claim acceleration from symmetric examples or a successful run when the final gap exceeds tolerance.
Add documented BSC and asymmetric-channel JSON examples and focused tests. Preserve the existing research code and clearly identify the new wrapper as a usability extension.
acceptance_checks: Malformed, empty, ragged, negative, nonfinite, and nonnormalized matrices fail with a concise actionable message.
A BSC with crossover probability 0.1 reports approximately 0.531004 bits per channel use within a documented numerical tolerance.
A deliberately small iteration limit produces an explicit unconverged result when its final gap exceeds the requested tolerance.
The existing numerical validation suite still passes, and README commands reproduce a result without editing Python source.

evidence.observation: blahut_arimoto converts W to a NumPy array and unpacks W.shape before computing probabilities; the inspected function has no explicit matrix validity checks.
accelerated_ba follows the same direct matrix conversion and returns the final gap and iteration count, which a wrapper can use to report convergence honestly.
The README documents the valid-channel assumptions, analytic examples, numerical test command, and distinct units for capacity and gap.
The inspected README describes SQLite notes, tags, search, and sharing through Android email intents. It provides Android unit, lint, and instrumentation verification commands.
The current daily digest reads top Hacker News stories and programming articles, without a user-interest ranking step.

alternatives.title: Investigate Markdown export for portable notes
alternatives.reason_not_selected: Potentially valuable, but the README alone does not prove export is absent. It needs a source-level review and Android verification before a concrete implementation recommendation.

alternatives.title: Rank reading links by project languages and interests
alternatives.reason_not_selected: A reasonable follow-up, but the digest was just launched and there is no feedback yet about which topics are most useful. The channel runner addresses a verified usability gap today.
